claim: The integrity of a Runx1/CBFβ holocomplex is crucial for NGF-dependent nonpeptidergic nociceptor maturation.
source: We show that the integrity of a Runx1/CBFβ holocomplex is crucial for NGF-dependent nonpeptidergic nociceptor maturation.
evidence: The claim is supported by genetic experiments showing that both Runx1 and CBFβ are required for nonpeptidergic nociceptor development, as demonstrated through conditional knockout studies and molecular analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: NGF signals through the ERK/MAPK pathway to promote expression of Cbfb but not Runx1 prior to maturation of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: NGF signals through the ERK/MAPK pathway to promote expression of Cbfb but not Runx1 prior to maturation of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological inhibition experiments with U0126, genetic loss-of-function studies in MAPK pathway mutants, and gain-of-function experiments with constitutively active B-Raf, as shown in Figure 7 and related analyses.

claim: Transcriptional initiation of Runx1 in nonpeptidergic nociceptor precursors is dependent on the homeodomain transcription factor Islet1.
source: In contrast, transcriptional initiation of Runx1 in nonpeptidergic nociceptor precursors is dependent on the homeodomain transcription factor Islet1, which is largely dispensable for Cbfb expression.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and microarray analysis showing that Runx1 transcripts are virtually undetectable in Isl1 CKO DRGs at E12.5, while Cbfb expression is minimally affected (Figure 8).

claim: Islet1 is largely dispensable for Cbfb expression.
source: In contrast, transcriptional initiation of Runx1 in nonpeptidergic nociceptor precursors is dependent on the homeodomain transcription factor Islet1, which is largely dispensable for Cbfb expression.
evidence: In situ hybridization and microarray analysis show that Cbfb expression is only minimally affected in Isl1 CKO animals (Figure 8C-E).

claim: The same Neurogenin1-dependent progenitor population gives rise to the three principal DRG neuron types within a relatively short time window.
source: Since the same Neurogenin1-dependent progenitor population gives rise to the three principal DRG neuron types within a relatively short time window (Frank and Sanes, 1991; Ma et al., 1999), specification of the diverse DRG neuron subtypes mainly takes place in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies by Frank and Sanes (1991) and Ma et al. (1999).

claim: Specification of the diverse DRG neuron subtypes mainly takes place in postmitotic neurons.
source: Since the same Neurogenin1-dependent progenitor population gives rise to the three principal DRG neuron types within a relatively short time window (Frank and Sanes, 1991; Ma et al., 1999), specification of the diverse DRG neuron subtypes mainly takes place in postmitotic neurons.
evidence: This is inferred from the fact that a single progenitor population gives rise to multiple neuron types within a short time window, as supported by cited literature.

claim: Peptidergic nociceptors are traditionally defined by expression of neuropeptides, such as CGRP and Substance P.
source: Peptidergic nociceptors are traditionally defined by expression of neuropeptides, such as CGRP and Substance P, while the majority of nonpeptidergic nociceptors have binding sites for the lectin IB4 (Mulderry et al., 1988; Silverman and Kruger, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Mulderry et al. (1988) and Silverman and Kruger (1990).

claim: The majority of nonpeptidergic nociceptors have binding sites for the lectin IB4.
source: Peptidergic nociceptors are traditionally defined by expression of neuropeptides, such as CGRP and Substance P, while the majority of nonpeptidergic nociceptors have binding sites for the lectin IB4 (Mulderry et al., 1988; Silverman and Kruger, 1990).
evidence: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by citations to Mulderry et al. (1988) and Silverman and Kruger (1990).

claim: A single cell transcriptome analysis led to the identification of four molecularly defined nonpeptidergic neuron subtypes.
source: More recently, a single cell transcriptome analysis led to the identification of four molecularly defined nonpeptidergic neuron subtypes (Usoskin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Usoskin et al. (2015).

claim: Nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors are preferentially required for mechanical and thermal nociception, respectively.
source: Functionally, nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors are preferentially required for mechanical and thermal nociception, respectively (Cavanaugh et al., 2009; McCoy et al., 2013; Mishra and Hoon, 2010; Vulchanova et al., 2001).
evidence: This functional distinction is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: Nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors derive from a common nociceptor precursor that expresses tropomyosin-receptor kinase A (TrkA).
source: Despite these differences, nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors derive from a common nociceptor precursor that expresses tropomyosin-receptor kinase A (TrkA), the receptor for nerve growth factor (NGF), and both nociceptor subtypes require NGF–TrkA signaling for survival and development beginning at ~E12.5 (Crowley et al., 1994; Luo et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2000; Silos-Santiago et al., 1995; Smeyne et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies demonstrating the common origin and NGF dependence.

claim: Both nociceptor subtypes require NGF–TrkA signaling for survival and development beginning at ~E12.5.
source: Despite these differences, nonpeptidergic and peptidergic nociceptors derive from a common nociceptor precursor that expresses tropomyosin-receptor kinase A (TrkA), the receptor for nerve growth factor (NGF), and both nociceptor subtypes require NGF–TrkA signaling for survival and development beginning at ~E12.5 (Crowley et al., 1994; Luo et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2000; Silos-Santiago et al., 1995; Smeyne et al., 1994).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous studies.

claim: The nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific switch from NGF responsiveness to GDNF family ligand (GFL) responsiveness occurs by virtue of the upregulation of Ret and GDNF family receptor alpha receptors (GFRα) starting from E15.5.
source: A key developmental event that defines the segregation of nociceptor subtypes is the nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific switch from NGF responsiveness to glial-derived neurotrophic factor (GDNF) family ligand (GFL) responsiveness. This occurs by virtue of the upregulation of Ret and GDNF family receptor alpha receptors (GFRα), receptor components for GFL signaling, in nonpeptidergic nociceptors starting from E15.5, as well as postnatal extinction of TrkA expression (Bennett et al., 1996; Bennett et al., 1998; Molliver and Snider, 1997; Molliver et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Bennett et al. (1996, 1998) and Molliver and colleagues (1997).

claim: Postnatal extinction of TrkA expression occurs in nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: This occurs by virtue of the upregulation of Ret and GDNF family receptor alpha receptors (GFRα), receptor components for GFL signaling, in nonpeptidergic nociceptors starting from E15.5, as well as postnatal extinction of TrkA expression (Bennett et al., 1996; Bennett et al., 1998; Molliver and Snider, 1997; Molliver et al., 1997).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: NGF–TrkA signaling is required for the acquisition of virtually all nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific features, including expression of Ret and Gfras.
source: Indeed, NGF–TrkA signaling is required for the acquisition of virtually all nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific features, including expression of Ret and Gfras, whereas GFL–GFRα/Ret signaling, in turn, plays a critical role in postnatal development of nonpeptidergic nociceptors, including expression of a subset of genes characteristic of mature nonpeptidergic nociceptors (Luo et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luo et al. (2007) and Patel et al. (2000).

claim: GFL–GFRα/Ret signaling plays a critical role in postnatal development of nonpeptidergic nociceptors, including expression of a subset of genes characteristic of mature nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: Indeed, NGF–TrkA signaling is required for the acquisition of virtually all nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific features, including expression of Ret and Gfras, whereas GFL–GFRα/Ret signaling, in turn, plays a critical role in postnatal development of nonpeptidergic nociceptors, including expression of a subset of genes characteristic of mature nonpeptidergic nociceptors (Luo et al., 2007; Patel et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Luo et al. (2007) and Patel et al. (2000).

claim: Runx1 expression is primarily restricted to nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: Most prominent is Runx1, a Runx family transcription factor whose expression is primarily restricted to nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by the literature and confirmed by the immunostaining data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Runx1 functions as a master regulator of the nonpeptidergic nociceptor lineage.
source: Runx1 functions as a master regulator of the nonpeptidergic nociceptor lineage (Chen et al., 2006; Yoshikawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al. (2006) and Yoshikawa et al. (2007).

claim: Runx proteins function as heterodimers by forming complexes with CBFβ, a non-DNA-binding cofactor.
source: In those systems, Runx proteins function as heterodimers by forming complexes with CBFβ, a non-DNA-binding cofactor that enhances the DNA binding affinity and protein stability of Runx proteins (Adya et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adya et al. (2000).

claim: CBFβ enhances the DNA binding affinity and protein stability of Runx proteins.
source: In those systems, Runx proteins function as heterodimers by forming complexes with CBFβ, a non-DNA-binding cofactor that enhances the DNA binding affinity and protein stability of Runx proteins (Adya et al., 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Adya et al. (2000).

claim: Genetic ablation of Runx1 leads to a near complete loss of nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific features and a concomitant expansion of neurons exhibiting a peptidergic nociceptor-like phenotype.
source: In the peripheral nervous system, genetic ablation of Runx1 leads to a near complete loss of nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific features and a concomitant expansion of neurons exhibiting a peptidergic nociceptor-like phenotype (Chen et al., 2006; Kramer et al., 2006; Yoshikawa et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al. (2006), Kramer et al. (2006), and Yoshikawa et al. (2007).

claim: The dramatic consequences of NGF deficiency on nonpeptidergic-specific gene expression resemble those seen upon Runx1 ablation.
source: Interestingly, the dramatic consequences of NGF deficiency on nonpeptidergic-specific gene expression resemble those seen upon Runx1 ablation (Chen et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Chen et al. (2006) and Luo et al. (2007).

claim: Expression of Mrgprd was almost completely abolished in presumptive nonpeptidergic nociceptors of both Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice at P0.
source: In accordance with previous observations, expression of the nonpeptidergic nociceptor markers Mrgprd and Gfra2 was almost completely abolished in presumptive nonpeptidergic nociceptors of both Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice at P0 (Figure 1A–D, K–N) (Chen et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1A-D and K-N, and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Expression of Gfra2 was almost completely abolished in presumptive nonpeptidergic nociceptors of both Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice at P0.
source: In accordance with previous observations, expression of the nonpeptidergic nociceptor markers Mrgprd and Gfra2 was almost completely abolished in presumptive nonpeptidergic nociceptors of both Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice at P0 (Figure 1A–D, K–N) (Chen et al., 2006; Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1, and supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Ptprt, Myo1a, and Kif21b exhibited dramatically reduced expression in neurons that would normally become nonpeptidergic nociceptors in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- mice compared to littermate controls at P0.
source: Moreover, newly identified nonpeptidergic-specific genes, including Ptprt, Myo1a, and Kif21b, exhibited dramatically reduced expression in neurons that would normally become nonpeptidergic nociceptors in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- mice compared to littermate controls at P0 (Figure 1E–J), in a manner similar to that observed in Runx1 CKO mice (Figure 1O–T).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1E-J.

claim: Impairment in expression of Mrgprd, Ptprt, Myo1a, and Kif21b was observed in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice as early as E16.5.
source: Furthermore, impairment in expression of Mrgprd, Ptprt, Myo1a, and Kif21b was observed in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- and Runx1 CKO mice as early as E16.5, which is when their expression is normally initiated (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Ret expression is severely impaired in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at P0.
source: Although Ret expression is severely impaired in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at P0, as previously described (Figure 2A–C) (Luo et al., 2007), its expression at this time point is only mildly affected in Runx1 CKO DRGs compared to controls, as shown by both in situ hybridization and real-time PCR (Figure 2F, G, J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2A-C, and supported by citation to Luo et al. (2007).

claim: Ret expression at P0 is only mildly affected in Runx1 CKO DRGs compared to controls.
source: Although Ret expression is severely impaired in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at P0, as previously described (Figure 2A–C) (Luo et al., 2007), its expression at this time point is only mildly affected in Runx1 CKO DRGs compared to controls, as shown by both in situ hybridization and real-time PCR (Figure 2F, G, J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 2F, G, J.

claim: NGF is required for initiation of Ret expression.
source: Therefore, while NGF is required for initiation of Ret expression, Runx1 is only required at a later stage, for maintenance of Ret expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the temporal analysis of Ret expression in NGF and Runx1 mutants showing early NGF dependence but delayed Runx1 dependence.

claim: Runx1 is only required at a later stage, for maintenance of Ret expression.
source: Therefore, while NGF is required for initiation of Ret expression, Runx1 is only required at a later stage, for maintenance of Ret expression.
evidence: This is inferred from the time-course analysis showing that Ret expression is normal at E16.5 in Runx1 CKO but becomes progressively impaired postnatally (Figure 2D-J).

claim: The level of NGF signaling, as assessed by the fluorescent intensity of phospho-Trk (pTrk) immunostaining, is lower in Runx1 CKO DRG neurons relative to controls at P0.
source: In fact, the level of NGF signaling, as assessed by the fluorescent intensity of phospho-Trk (pTrk) immunostaining, is lower in Runx1 CKO DRG neurons relative to controls at P0 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-F.

claim: TrkA levels in control and Runx1 CKO DRGs are indistinguishable at P0.
source: This ability of Runx1 to sustain normal levels of TrkA activity is not simply due to an effect on TrkA expression, as TrkA levels in control and Runx1 CKO DRGs are indistinguishable, as determined by immunohistochemistry (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunohistochemistry data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, H.

claim: Ret expression appears normal at E16.5 in Runx1 CKO mice.
source: However, since Ret expression, which is strongly dependent on NGF signaling in nonpeptidergic nociceptors, appears normal at E16.5 (Figure 2D, E), it is unlikely that diminished NGF signaling observed at P0 accounts for the profound deficits in initiation of expression of nonpeptidergic-specific genes in E16.5 Runx1 CKO mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 2D, E.

claim: Exogenous NGF administration fails to rescue nonpeptidergic nociceptor gene expression deficits in Runx1 CKO DRGs, with the notable exception of Ret.
source: With the notable exception of Ret, whose expression was partially restored following NGF injection into Runx1 CKO mice (Figure 3J–L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2D), we found a general and complete lack of effect of NGF administration on expression of nonpeptidergic-specific genes in Runx1 CKO DRGs (Figure 3A–I and Figure 3—figure supplement 2A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 3A-L and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: NGF treatment led to a robust increase in expression of Mrgprd, Gfra2, and Ptprt in wildtype neurons but not in Runx1-deficient neurons.
source: Importantly, NGF treatment led to a robust increase in expression of the nonpeptidergic-specific genes, Mrgprd, Gfra2, and Ptprt, in wildtype neurons but not in Runx1-deficient neurons (Figure 2M–O).
evidence: This is demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis of dissociated DRG cultures shown in Figure 3M-O.

claim: Ret expression was NGF-dependent in both control and Runx1-deficient neurons, albeit to a lesser extent in the absence of Runx1.
source: In contrast, Ret expression was NGF-dependent in both control and Runx1-deficient neurons, albeit to a lesser extent in the absence of Runx1 (Figure 3P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis shown in Figure 3P.

claim: Cbfb is expressed at varying levels in the majority, if not all, DRG neurons over the entire time course of analysis.
source: In situ hybridization analysis revealed that Cbfb is expressed at varying levels, in the majority, if not all, DRG neurons over the entire time course of our analysis (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Flag-CBFβ appears to be expressed in nearly all DRG neurons, at varying levels.
source: In CbfbFlag mice, the Flag antibody allows for specific detection of endogenous Flag-CBFβ, which appears to be expressed in nearly all DRG neurons, at varying levels (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Flag immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A, B.

claim: Double labeling of Flag and Runx1 showed overlap between CBFβ and Runx1 throughout nociceptor development.
source: Double labeling of Flag and Runx1 showed overlap between CBFβ and Runx1 throughout nociceptor development suggesting a potential interaction between these two proteins (Figure 4C–E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E–G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C-E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1E-G.

claim: CBFβ is broadly expressed and found in more than just Runx1+ neurons.
source: It is noteworthy that CBFβ is broadly expressed and found in more than just Runx1+ neurons, suggesting additional Runx1-independent CBFβ functions in the DRG (Figure 4C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by double immunostaining data showing CBFβ expression in neurons that do not express Runx1 (Figure 4C-E).

claim: Runx1 is enriched in Flag immunoprecipitates from CbfbFlag/Flag animals but not wildtype animals.
source: Indeed, Runx1 is enriched in Flag immunoprecipitates from CbfbFlag/Flag animals but not wildtype animals (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Runx1 and CBFβ are co-expressed and form a complex in developing DRG neurons.
source: Thus, Runx1 and CBFβ are co-expressed and form a complex in developing DRG neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by co-immunoprecipitation experiments and double immunostaining data (Figure 4).

claim: Cbfb CKO animals exhibit a wide range of nonpeptidergic nociceptor phenotypes that are virtually identical to those seen in Runx1 CKO mice.
source: Analysis of Wnt1-Cre; Cbfbf/f (Cbfb CKO) animals revealed a wide range of nonpeptidergic nociceptor phenotypes that are virtually identical to those seen in Runx1 CKO mice.
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR analysis showing similar gene expression deficits in both mutants (Figure 5A-J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D, E).

claim: Expression of CGRP, a marker of peptidergic nociceptors, was de-repressed in Cbfb CKO animals.
source: As has been shown for Runx1 CKO animals, expression of CGRP, a marker of peptidergic nociceptors, was de-repressed in Cbfb CKO animals (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data are not shown.

claim: Cbfb CKO animals at P0 exhibited a marked reduction of sensory innervation of the epidermis.
source: Furthermore, like Runx1 CKO mice, Cbfb CKO animals at P0 exhibited a marked reduction of sensory innervation of the epidermis (Figure 5K–P).
evidence: This is demonstrated by GFP immunostaining of skin sections shown in Figure 5K-P.

claim: The epidermal innervation defect in Cbfb CKO mice was primarily due to a deficiency in the peripheral projections of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: This defect was primarily due to a deficiency in the peripheral projections of nonpeptidergic nociceptors, considering the sparseness of epidermal innervation by peptidergic nociceptors at P0 as well as their unperturbed innervation pattern in the absence of CBFβ (data not shown).
evidence: This is inferred from the known innervation patterns of different nociceptor subtypes and the observation that peptidergic innervation is unaffected.

claim: The subepidermal nerve plexus is unaffected in Cbfb CKO mice.
source: We also found that the subepidermal nerve plexus is unaffected in Cbfb CKO mice, indicating a developmental defect in the final stage of peripheral target innervation.
evidence: This is stated based on observations of the nerve plexus.

claim: Following postnatal deletion of either Runx1 or Cbfb, few or no tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)+ C-low threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs) were observed during the third postnatal week.
source: However, following postnatal deletion of either Runx1 or Cbfb, we observed, during the third postnatal week, few or no tyrosine hydroxylase (TH)+  C-low threshold mechanoreceptors (C-LTMRs), a nonpeptidergic neuronal subtype (Li et al., 2011; Seal et al., 2009).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-M.

claim: Key features of C-LTMRs, including TH expression and longitudinal lanceolate endings in the periphery, are nearly completely absent in mice lacking Runx1 or CBFβ at postnatal time points.
source: Specifically, key features of C-LTMRs, including TH expression and longitudinal lanceolate endings in the periphery, as marked by expression of a Cre-dependent GFP reporter (Hippenmeyer et al., 2005), are nearly completely absent in mice lacking Runx1 or CBFβ at postnatal time points (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-M.

claim: There is a dramatic defect in Runx1 protein expression in Cbfb CKO DRGs at P0.
source: The phenocopy of Runx1 and Cbfb mutants may be partly attributed to a dramatic defect in Runx1 protein expression in Cbfb CKO DRGs, as shown by immunostaining and western blot analysis at P0 (Figure 5Q–S).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and western blot data shown in Figure 5Q-S.

claim: The Runx1 protein deficit in Cbfb CKO DRGs was evident as early as E13.
source: This Runx1 protein deficit was evident as early as E13 (data not shown).
evidence: This is stated in the text but data are not shown.

claim: Runx1 mRNA expression remained unchanged, if not increased, in Cbfb CKO DRGs compared to controls.
source: Runx1 mRNA expression, on the other hand, remained unchanged, if not increased, in Cbfb CKO DRGs compared to controls, as determined by both in situ hybridization and real-time PCR (Figure 5T–V).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 5T-V.

claim: CBFβ plays a key role in the post-transcriptional regulation of Runx1 expression, most likely at the level of protein stability.
source: These findings demonstrate a key role for CBFβ in the post-transcriptional regulation of Runx1 expression, most likely at the level of protein stability.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that Runx1 mRNA is normal or increased while Runx1 protein is dramatically reduced in Cbfb CKO DRGs.

claim: Cbfb mRNA expression was significantly reduced in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs relative to controls at E14.5, specifically in small-diameter nociceptor precursors.
source: In fact, at E14.5, a time prior to expression of nonpeptidergic nociceptor-specific genes, Cbfb mRNA expression was significantly reduced in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs relative to controls, specifically in small-diameter nociceptor precursors (Figure 6A, B, E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6A, B, E.

claim: The Cbfb expression deficit in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- small diameter DRG neurons becomes much more pronounced at E16.5.
source: This Cbfb expression deficit in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- small diameter DRG neurons becomes much more pronounced at later time stages, such as E16.5, the onset of observable deficits in nonpeptidergic-specific gene expression (Figure 6C–E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 6C-E.

claim: Ntrk1-/-/Bax-/- DRGs displayed reduced levels of Cbfb expression at P0.
source: Similarly, Ntrk1-/-/Bax-/- DRGsdisplayed reduced levels of Cbfb expression at P0 (Figure 7H, I).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7H, I.

claim: NGF is essential for CBFβ protein expression in vitro.
source: First, Flag immunostaining on dissociated DRG cultures from P0 CbfbFlag/+  animals showed that NGF is essential for CBFβ protein expression in vitro (Figure 6F–H).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Flag immunostaining of dissociated DRG cultures shown in Figure 6F-H.

claim: The level of Flag immunoreactivity was significantly lower in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- neurons compared to controls in acutely dissociated DRGs from P0 animals.
source: Second, when DRGs from P0 control and Ngf-/-; Bax-/- animals that were also heterozygous for the CbfbFlag allele were acutely dissociated, the level of Flag immunoreactivity was significantly lower in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- neurons compared to controls, suggesting NGF-dependence of CBFβ protein expression in vivo (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Flag immunostaining of acutely dissociated DRG neurons shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-D.

claim: Cbfb is sensitive to the dose of NGF as exogenous NGF administered to wildtype neonates via intraperitoneal injection further potentiated Cbfb expression.
source: Cbfb is also sensitive to the dose of NGF as exogenous NGF administered to wildtype neonates via intraperitoneal injection further potentiated Cbfb expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by real-time PCR analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Runx1 mRNA levels are normal in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at E14.5.
source: On the other hand, Runx1 mRNA levels are normal in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at E14.5, as determined by both in situ hybridization and real-time PCR analysis (Figure 6I, J, M), consistent with our previous observation (Luo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6I, J, M, and supported by citation to Luo et al. (2007).

claim: Runx1 expression becomes affected beginning at E16.5, suggesting a late requirement of NGF for maintenance of Runx1 expression.
source: It is only at later times, beginning at E16.5, that Runx1 expression becomes affected, suggesting a late requirement of NGF for maintenance of Runx1 expression (Figure 6K–M).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization and real-time PCR data shown in Figure 6K-M.

claim: Runx1 protein expression is unaffected in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at E14.5.
source: Consistent with the late NGF dependence of Runx1 mRNA expression, Runx1 protein expression is unaffected in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at E14.5 (Figure 6N, O, R, S).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Runx1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 6N, O, R, S.

claim: At E16.5, the level of Runx1 protein is significantly diminished without any change in the number of Runx1+ neurons.
source: At E16.5, the level of Runx1 protein is significantly diminished without any change in the number of Runx1+ neurons (Figure 6P–S).
evidence: This is demonstrated by Runx1 immunostaining data shown in Figure 6P-S.

claim: Pharmacological inactivation of Mek1/2 greatly attenuated the ability of NGF to promote CBFβ protein expression in vitro.
source: Through immunostaining and immunoblot analysis, we found that pharmacological inactivation of Mek1/2, direct activators of ERK1/2, greatly attenuated the ability of NGF to promote CBFβ protein expression in vitro (Figure 7A–E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is demonstrated by immunostaining and immunoblot data shown in Figure 7A-E and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: In 4 out of 5 P0 Nes-Cre; Map2k1f/f;Map2k2-/-; Mapk3-/-; Mapk1f/f mutants (Quadruple), Cbfb mRNA expression was severely disrupted.
source: Using this in vivo model system, we found that in 4 out of 5 P0 Nes-Cre; Map2k1f/f;Map2k2-/-; Mapk3-/-; Mapk1f/f mutants (Quadruple), Cbfb mRNA expression was severely disrupted, demonstrating a strong dependence of Cbfb expression on MAPK signaling in vivo (Figure 7F, G).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7F, G.

claim: While Cbfb expression in Ntrk1-/-; Bax-/- DRGs was severely impaired, expression of B-RafV600E in Ntrk1-/-; Bax-/- mice to promote constitutive MAPK signaling restored Cbfb expression to near normal levels.
source: Remarkably, while Cbfb expression in Ntrk1-/-; Bax-/- DRGs was severely impaired, expression of B-RafV600E in Ntrk1-/-; Bax-/- mice to promote constitutive MAPK signaling restored Cbfb expression to near normal levels (Figure 7H–J).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 7H-J.

claim: The ERK/MAPK signaling cascade is both necessary and sufficient to mediate NGF/TrkA-dependent expression of Cbfb.
source: Together, these findings indicate that the ERK/MAPK signaling cascade is both necessary and sufficient to mediate NGF/TrkA-dependent expression of Cbfb.
evidence: This is concluded from the combined loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments demonstrating MAPK's role in Cbfb expression.

claim: Runx1 transcripts were virtually undetectable in Isl1 CKO DRGs at E12.5.
source: Consistent with a central role for Islet in initiating Runx1 expression at the transcriptional level, Runx1 transcripts were virtually undetectable in Isl1 CKO DRGs (Figure 8A, B).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8A, B.

claim: Cbfb expression was only minimally affected by Islet1 deficiency at E12.5.
source: In contrast, Cbfb expression was only minimally affected by the same genetic perturbation (Figure 8C, D).
evidence: This is demonstrated by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 8C, D.

claim: The distinct dependence of Runx1 and Cbfb expression on Islet1 was confirmed by a microarray analysis of control and Isl1 CKO DRGs at E12.5.
source: The distinct dependence of Runx1 and Cbfb expression on Islet1 was confirmed by a microarray analysis of control and Isl1 CKO DRGs at E12.5 (Figure 8E).
evidence: This is demonstrated by microarray data shown in Figure 8E.

claim: The Runx1/CBFβ complex serves as a coincidence detector for extrinsic and intrinsic signals that promote specification of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: The Runx1/CBFβ holocomplex therefore serves as a coincidence detector for extrinsic and intrinsic signals that promote specification of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the findings that Runx1 and Cbfb are differentially regulated by Islet1 and NGF, respectively, and both are required for nonpeptidergic nociceptor development.

claim: The requirement for NGF ensures that only those nociceptor precursors that gain access to a sufficient amount of NGF and survive the period of naturally occurring cell death will undergo nonpeptidergic nociceptor maturation.
source: The requirement for NGF, an extrinsic cue that is critical for survival of all nociceptors, ensures that only those nociceptor precursors that gain access to a sufficient amount of NGF and survive the period of naturally occurring cell death will undergo nonpeptidergic nociceptor maturation.
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation of the role of NGF in nonpeptidergic nociceptor development.

claim: Cbfb expression exhibits NGF dependence at E14.5, immediately following the period of naturally occurring cell death.
source: Consistent with this, Cbfb expression exhibits NGF dependence at E14.5, immediately following the period of naturally occurring cell death.
evidence: This is based on the in situ hybridization data showing Cbfb expression deficits in Ngf-/-; Bax-/- DRGs at E14.5 (Figure 6A, B, E).

claim: The dependence of Runx1 expression on Islet1 likely contributes to the orderly transition from pan-sensory neurogenesis to specification of nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: On the other hand, the dependence of Runx1 expression on Islet1, a transcription factor required for terminating expression of genes whose expression is restricted to the early stage of sensory neurogenesis, likely contributes to the orderly transition from pan-sensory neurogenesis to specification of nonpeptidergic nociceptors by ensuring that Runx1 expression and hence Runx1/CBFβ-dependent nonpeptidergic nociceptor development are initiated after sensory neurogenesis (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a conceptual interpretation supported by citation to Sun et al. (2008) regarding Islet1's role in sensory neurogenesis.

claim: NGF and Islet1 signals coordinate temporal control of the Runx1/CBFβ complex for timely initiation of nonpeptidergic nociceptor differentiation.
source: Thus the NGF and Islet1 signals coordinate temporal control of the Runx1/CBFβ complex for timely initiation of nonpeptidergic nociceptor differentiation.
evidence: This is a conceptual conclusion drawn from the differential regulation of Runx1 and Cbfb by Islet1 and NGF.

claim: NGF and Islet1 are unlikely to be sufficient to instruct Runx1/CBFβ complex formation and the nonpeptidergic nociceptor lineage choice.
source: It is important to note that the extrinsic and intrinsic signals described here are unlikely to be sufficient to instruct Runx1/CBFβ complex formation and the nonpeptidergic nociceptor lineage choice, as neither NGF nor Islet1 functions exclusively in nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
evidence: This is inferred from the known broader functions of NGF and Islet1 in DRG development.

claim: NGF–TrkA signaling is required for survival, target innervation and normal phenotypic development of both peptidergic and nonpeptidergic nociceptors.
source: Indeed, NGF–TrkA signaling is required for survival, target innervation and normal phenotypic development of both peptidergic and nonpeptidergic nociceptors (Harrington and Ginty, 2013), and Islet1 is expressed broadly in developing DRG neurons and is required for the generation of virtually all nociceptors (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Harrington and Ginty (2013) and Sun et al. (2008).

claim: Islet1 is expressed broadly in developing DRG neurons and is required for the generation of virtually all nociceptors.
source: Indeed, NGF–TrkA signaling is required for survival, target innervation and normal phenotypic development of both peptidergic and nonpeptidergic nociceptors (Harrington and Ginty, 2013), and Islet1 is expressed broadly in developing DRG neurons and is required for the generation of virtually all nociceptors (Sun et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sun et al. (2008).

claim: One or more additional, unidentified signals must govern the divergence of the two main nociceptive lineages.
source: Therefore, one or more additional, unidentified signals must govern the divergence of the two main nociceptive lineages.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the observation that NGF and Islet1 are not specific to nonpeptidergic nociceptors.

claim: MAPK signaling may play a similar role in controlling Cbfb expression in cells outside of the nervous system.
source: The generality of MAPK signaling suggests that it plays a similar role in controlling Cbfb expression in cells outside of the nervous system and thus MAPK–CBFβ signaling may have a general role in cell type specification.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the findings to other cell types.

claim: MAPK–CBFβ signaling may have a general role in cell type specification.
source: The generality of MAPK signaling suggests that it plays a similar role in controlling Cbfb expression in cells outside of the nervous system and thus MAPK–CBFβ signaling may have a general role in cell type specification.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the generality of MAPK signaling.

claim: CREB family members may be direct transcriptional activators of Cbfb.
source: To this end, we found, through bioinformatic analysis of the putative Cbfb promoter, cAMP-response element (CRE) consensus motifs within an evolutionally conserved 458 bp enhancer-like element (data not shown), raising the intriguing possibility that CREB family members, which are well-studied downstream mediators of MAPK signaling in many cell types (Shaywitz and Greenberg, 1999), are direct transcriptional activators of Cbfb.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on bioinformatic analysis and known functions of CREB, supported by citation to Shaywitz and Greenberg (1999).

claim: Common effectors of growth factor signaling pathways support distinct biological outcomes by controlling expression of distinct target genes.
source: In view of the role of CREB family members in NGF-dependent growth and survival of neurons (Liu et al., 1999; Riccio et al., 1999), the possibility of CREB-mediated activation of Cbfb expression would further suggest that common effectors of growth factor signaling pathways support distinct biological outcomes, in this case, survival, axon growth and maturation of nociceptors, presumably by controlling expression of distinct target genes.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation supported by citations to Liu et al. (1999) and Riccio et al. (1999).

claim: Convergence of extrinsic and intrinsic signals onto a single heterodimeric transcription factor complex controls lineage-specific differentiation programs and postmitotic specification of neuronal subtypes.
source: The gene regulatory mechanism described here leads us to propose a simple model in which convergence of extrinsic and intrinsic signals onto a single heterodimeric transcription factor complex controls lineage-specific differentiation programs and postmitotic specification of neuronal subtypes (Figure 8F).
evidence: This is a conceptual model proposed based on the findings of the study, illustrated in Figure 8F.

claim: This model is conceivably generally applicable to a broad range of neuronal subtypes that rely on heterodimeric transcription factor complexes for their specification.
source: It is conceivable that this simple model is generally applicable to a broad range of neuronal subtypes that rely on heterodimeric transcription factor complexes for their specification.
evidence: This is a speculative extension of the model to other neuronal subtypes.

claim: In control DRGs at P0, 12.7% ± 2.4% of neurons express Mrgprd, while in Ngf-/-Bax-/- DRGs, 0% express Mrgprd.
source: (A–J) Expression of Mrgprd (Control, 12.7% ± 2.4%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 0%), Gfra2 (Control, 28.7% ± 2.5%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 14.3% ± 1.1%), Ptprt (Control, 19.1% ± 0.3%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 10.3% ± 2.1%), Myo1a (Control, 26.4% ± 0.9%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 5.8% ± 1.5%) and Kif21b (Control, 27.2% ± 2.7%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 14.05% ± 1.8%) in control and Ngf-/-Bax-/- DRGs at P0, assessed by in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is quantitative data from in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 1A-J.

claim: In control DRGs at P0, 28.7% ± 2.5% of neurons express Gfra2, while in Ngf-/-Bax-/- DRGs, 14.3% ± 1.1% express Gfra2.
source: (A–J) Expression of Mrgprd (Control, 12.7% ± 2.4%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 0%), Gfra2 (Control, 28.7% ± 2.5%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 14.3% ± 1.1%), Ptprt (Control, 19.1% ± 0.3%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 10.3% ± 2.1%), Myo1a (Control, 26.4% ± 0.9%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 5.8% ± 1.5%) and Kif21b (Control, 27.2% ± 2.7%; Ngf-/-Bax-/-, 14.05% ± 1.8%) in control and Ngf-/-Bax-/- DRGs at P0, assessed by in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is quantitative data from in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 1.

claim: In control DRGs at P0, 26.3% ± 1.0% of neurons express Mrgprd, while in Runx1 CKO DRGs, 0.3% ± 0.2% express Mrgprd.
source: (K–T) Expression of Mrgprd (Control, 26.3% ± 1.0%; Runx1 CKO, 0.3% ± 0.2%), Gfra2 (Control, 40.0% ± 3.7%; Runx1 CKO, 9.6% ± 0.7%), Ptprt (Control, 36.0% ± 3.3%; Runx1 CKO, 10.4% ± 2.3%), Myo1a (Control, 31.1% ± 2.3%; Runx1 CKO, 5.1% ± 1.8%) and Kif21b (Control, 24.8% ± 1.7%; Runx1 CKO, 10.9% ± 0.8%) in control and Runx1 CKO DRGs at P0, assessed by in situ hybridization.
evidence: This is quantitative data from in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 1K-T.

claim: In control DRGs at P0, 26.9% ± 2.8% of neurons express Mrgprd, while in Cbfb CKO DRGs, 0% express Mrgprd.
source: (A–J) Expression of Mrgprd (Control, 26.9% ± 2.8%; Cbfb CKO, 0%), Gfra2 (Control, 38.8% ± 2.8%; Cbfb CKO, 11.7% ± 1.9%), Ptprt, (Control, 31.9% ± 3.2%; Cbfb CKO, 7.1% ± 2.8%), Myo1a (Control, 26.9% ± 3.2%; Cbfb CKO, 5.6% ± 0.6%) and Kif21b (Control, 20.2% ± 0.1%; Cbfb CKO, 2.4% ± 0.5%) in control and Cbfb CKO DRGs at P0 by in situ hybridization analysis.
evidence: This is quantitative data from in situ hybridization analysis shown in Figure 5A-J.

claim: In control animals at P21, 23.2% ± 1.6% of GFP+ neurons express TH, while in Runx1 mutant animals, 3.8% ± 2.7% express TH.
source: (F-I) Expression of TH and GFP in DRGs of P21 Runx1CreER/ + ; TaumGFP/ +  and Runx1CreER/f; TaumGFP/ +  animals (F and G)(Control, 23.2% ± 1.6%; Runx1 mutant, 3.8% ± 2.7%) or Runx1CreER/ + ;Cbfbf/ + ; TaumGFP/ +  and Runx1CreER/ + ; Cbfbf/f; TaumGFP/ +  animals (H and I) (Control, 21.4% ± 1.9%; Cbfb mutant, 8.9% ± 2.0%) that received an intraperitoneal injection of tamoxifen at P2.
evidence: This is quantitative data from immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F-I.
